accuracy.evidence: Checked against the named sources: Holman, Garfin and Silver 2014 (PNAS) found 6+ hours a day of Boston Marathon bombing coverage went with higher acute stress than direct exposure; Pfefferbaum et al. 2001 linked more TV coverage with more stress symptoms in children far from Oklahoma City; Childline and BBC Newsround advise that feeling upset is normal, take a break, talk to a trusted adult, use trusted sources; AAP and APA family guidance (ask what they saw, honest facts, reassurance, look for the helpers); DfE Health Education 2019 (where to seek support, not all online content is accurate); Full Fact notes old images are often reshared as new. The flood story is fictional and the worry meter is labelled in the adult text as a picture, not a measure.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented slips: worry means something is wrong with me (scene 1 prediction, challenge q1); watching more will bring calm (scene 2 prediction and rising meter, challenge q2); pretending to be fine or keeping it secret (the 'nothing, I am fine' and 'please don't tell anyone' cards are refused in scene 3, challenge q5 and q7); comments and rumours as facts (feed clips 3-4, challenge q3); a widely shared photo must be new (scene 4 prediction and the 2019 photo fact, challenge q4); passing a scary clip to a younger child (sort card, challenge q6); scrolling at bedtime (sort card, challenge q7).

lab_distinct.evidence: The lab is built round this topic's own moment, a news video and what to do next: tap worry signs on Rami while a worry cloud grows; swipe an autoplay feed whose clips (same flood again, a scary comment, a rumour, added music) push a worry meter up until the phone is dragged to the table; fill 'I saw / It made me feel / I want to know' gaps with refusal of pretend, more and secret chips; match 4 'what if?' questions to checked facts (map, helpers, photo date, family plan). Lab-distinct gate passes under 30% overlap with every flagship, including flagtrust (858), flagcalm and flagfeed; none has a feed, a worry meter or a fact-check match.

lab_teaches.evidence: The learner meets each idea before the text names it: the meter climbs with every swipe and freezes only when the phone goes down; the pretend and secret chips are refused with a reason; matching the photo question lands on 'That photo is from 2019. Someone shared it again'. Each step's done text (LEARNT) then states the rule: stop, tell, check, calm.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with tempting wrong options the lab disproves: 'Yes, he should not feel like that' (scene 1 shows these are common worry signs and names the feeling); 'Yes: knowing more will calm him down' (each extra video pushes the meter up); 'Yes: people only share new photos' (the checked fact shows a 2019 photo reshared).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Seven questions rotate and every wrong option maps to a named slip in slip(): wrongfeel, more, pretend, secret, rumour, old, share and bed, each one sentence naming the mistake and the better move (for example 'Old photos and videos are often shared again as if they are new. A grown-up can check the date.'). Feedback is shown in a role=status live region with a Next one button.

readability.evidence: Kid paragraphs read at FK grade 0.7-2.4 (family kid limit 5.0) with short sentences and concrete words (tight tummy, put the phone down, worries are not secrets); the adult text reads at grade 8.8 overall, under the 10.0 limit in learn/validate_lessons.py. Canvas labels are short ('Table: put the phone here', 'I want to know… could it happen here?') and each feedback line is one or two sentences.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate is clean. Each kid paragraph does one job: name the feeling; stop watching; tell without pretending; check facts and calm down. Adult paragraphs give the evidence on repeated exposure, the consistent advice from Childline, Newsround, AAP/APA and DfE, the common mistakes with the meter caveat, and how the lesson differs from the related telling, calming and misinformation lessons.

mobile.evidence: Checked iPhone 13 screenshots of every scene before and after Show me, plus a 1200 px desktop in dark theme. Fixed two problems found on screenshots: the worry cloud grew over the title, so it was shrunk and moved beside the head; matched questions vanished and left lines from empty space, so they now stay in place, ticked, with lines from their right edge. Real pointer drags at 390 px worked for a sign tap, a swipe-up on the phone, a chip into the 'I saw' gap, a question onto its fact and a card into the Helps box.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a labelled button twin: 'Worry sign? …' per card, 'Swipe to the next video' and 'Put the phone down', one button per chip and gap, one per question and fact, and Helps / Bigger buttons per sort card, each with a full-sentence aria-label. The canvas aria-label carries the instructions, each result and every refusal; challenge feedback is role=status; ticks, 'Worry:' prefixes and counts mark state as well as colour. The browser gate runs axe (WCAG 2.1 AA) in both themes on desktop and iPhone 13.

sources: Holman EA, Garfin DR, Silver RC (2014) Media's role in broadcasting acute stress following the Boston Marathon bombings. PNAS 111: 93-98
Pfefferbaum B et al. (2001) Television exposure in children after a terrorist incident. Psychiatry 64: 202-211
